top_choice_rationale: P001 (B038: Autor, Hanson, Dorn) rewards a specific, well-identified discovery: import and technology exposure produce large, concentrated and persistent local labour-market adjustment costs. It combines newly assembled data with a transparent design and has had over a decade of independent replication, critique and extension, so durability can actually be judged. The round-2 exchange settled attribution on the empirical core, with Dorn rather than Katz as the third name. The citation is limited to the empirical analysis of exposure and local adjustment and does not claim the task framework, whose lineage (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu) lies outside the trio. The shift-share critique and the debate over magnitudes are a real discount on point estimates, but they refine the conditions for valid inference without overturning the qualitative finding. P003 (B002) is a close second: its measurement and design are excellent, but its core results are about a decade old, depend on restricted data, and have credit spread across a large team. P004 (B013) is conceptually deep and cleanly attributed, but the empirical record of its specific predictions is mixed. P002 (B001) is mature and cleanly attributed, but its empirical content is indirect and earlier game-theory prizes overlap. P005 (B041) has the most contested attribution. No award is ranked last because several candidates are clearly prize-worthy.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. No frequent co-author (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) is credited on any proposal. I work in quasi-experimental labour economics, which is close to B038 and B002, and I treat that as field familiarity, not merit. I presented the 2023 prize (Goldin), which reflects Academy drafting and is relevant only to prior-prize overlap. I sit on the American Economic Review board of editors, with no personal tie to any candidate.
